core: Aspect ratio as the width-to-height shape of a graphic (e.g., 1:1, 4:5, 9:16, 16:9), distinct from pixel dimensions
Why aspect ratio matters: a mismatched ratio forces the platform to crop, letterbox, or stretch the image, and the right ratio fills more of the screen in the feed
The four common social ratios and their roles: square 1:1 and portrait 4:5 for feeds, vertical 9:16 for full-screen stories/reels, landscape 16:9 for wide/desktop video
Designing for small screens and fast-scrolling feeds: one bold focal point, large legible type, and high contrast so the graphic reads at a glance
Safe zones: keeping key text and elements in the central region, clear of interface overlays (username/timestamp at the top, caption and action buttons at the bottom and side)
Brand consistency across platforms using templates that fix colors, fonts, and logo placement
Static graphics versus animated/video graphics as a format choice
Accessibility basics for social graphics: descriptive alt text, captions on video, and not relying on color alone (WCAG owns the detailed standards; this lesson names them and hands off)
Exact pixel dimensions vary by platform and change over time, so designers work from principles and aspect ratios rather than memorizing numbers
supporting: 1080 pixels wide is a common working width across major platforms, though exact specs differ and change
Vertical, mobile-first ratios (4:5, 9:16) tend to occupy more of a phone screen than square or landscape, which is why they are favored in feeds
The safe-zone idea descends from the broadcast 'title-safe / action-safe' convention for keeping content away from screen edges
Captions on video benefit Deaf and hard-of-hearing viewers and also serve the very common case of watching with sound off
Alt text is authored per image based on its context and function, not a fixed caption
outOfScope: The full WCAG success criteria and exact contrast thresholds, owned by the Accessibility in Graphic Design topic (named and handed off here)
Brand identity strategy, brand voice, and logo design, owned by the Branding and Logo Design topics
The catalogue of image file formats (JPEG/PNG/WebP/etc.), owned by the File Formats topic
Pixels-per-inch, resolution, and dimensions as such, owned by the Image Resolution topic
Platform-specific, dated pixel dimensions and per-network upload rules, which change frequently and are deliberately not memorized here

claims.claim: An aspect ratio expresses the proportional relationship between an image's width and height (written as two numbers with a colon, such as 16:9, 4:5, or 1:1) and describes its shape, which is different from pixel dimensions that give an exact size.

If a graphic's aspect ratio does not match what a platform expects, the platform must crop, add bars (letterbox), or stretch it, none of which look good; the right ratio also lets the content occupy more of the screen in a feed, increasing the chance a scroller stops on it.

Common social aspect ratios map to formats: square 1:1 and portrait 4:5 dominate feeds, vertical 9:16 is the primary full-screen format for stories and reels, and 16:9 is the landscape ratio for wide/desktop-oriented content; vertical, mobile-first ratios (4:5, 9:16) tend to fill more of a phone screen than square or landscape.

Exact pixel dimensions vary by platform and change over time (platforms 'change up how images display' repeatedly), so 1080 pixels wide is a common working width but the durable skill is designing to aspect ratios and principles rather than memorizing per-platform numbers.

On small phone screens in fast-scrolling feeds, a graphic needs a clear visual hierarchy with a single dominant focal point, large legible type, and strong contrast so the most important element is seen first and the message reads at a glance.

Interface elements sit on top of full-screen social graphics: usernames and timestamps near the top, and captions, action buttons, and reply bars along the bottom and side, so key text and imagery should be kept inside a central 'safe zone' clear of those overlays and of edge crops.

Images that convey information must have text alternatives (alt text) that describe the information or function of the image; alt text is determined by the author based on the image's usage, context, and content, and it lets screen-reader users, speech-input users, and others access the content.

Captions are a synchronized text version of the speech and important non-speech audio in a video, displayed in the player; they are required for prerecorded video audio at WCAG Level A, benefit people who are Deaf or hard of hearing and those who process text better than audio, and also serve viewers watching with sound off. (Captions are same-language; subtitles translate audio into another language.)

Designers should not rely on color alone to convey meaning, and social graphics should meet accessibility guidance; the detailed WCAG standards (contrast ratios, success criteria) are a separate accessibility topic that this lesson names and defers to rather than restating in full.

Brand consistency across platforms is achieved by reusing templates that fix colors, typefaces, and logo placement, so a set of posts reads as one identity regardless of which network or format it appears in.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Which single aspect ratio is 'best' for feed posts.
positions: Square 1:1 maximizes cross-platform consistency and is a safe default.
Portrait 4:5 occupies more vertical space on phones and tends to outperform square in mobile feeds.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents both as valid feed ratios with a trade-off (consistency vs. screen real estate) rather than declaring one universally best, and notes vertical/mobile-first ratios generally fill more of a phone screen.

sourceRecords.title: Images Tutorial: Text Alternatives
sourceRecords.notes: W3C WAI tutorial read on 2026-08-19 via WebFetch. Supports: images must have text alternatives that describe the information or function represented by them; the text alternative is determined by the author depending on the usage, context, and content of an image; beneficiaries include screen-reader users (read aloud or Braille), speech-input users, speech-enabled browsing, and mobile users. Grounds the alt-text guidance for social graphics. Reference-only; no wording reproduced, all prose original.

sourceRecords.title: Captions/Subtitles
sourceRecords.notes: W3C WAI page read on 2026-08-19 via WebFetch. Supports: captions are a text version of the speech and non-speech audio information needed to understand the content, displayed within the media player and synchronized with the audio; required in WCAG at Level A for prerecorded video audio; benefit people who are Deaf and hard of hearing and those who process written information better than audio; captions are for the same language as the spoken audio while subtitles translate into another language. Also grounds the sound-off use case. Reference-only; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Social media image sizes for all networks
sourceRecords.notes: Regularly-updated industry reference read on 2026-08-19 via WebFetch, used REFERENCE_ONLY to ground current aspect-ratio conventions and their volatility. Supports: aspect ratio is the proportional shape of an image versus its pixel size; feed posts favor 1:1 and 4:5, stories/reels use 9:16, landscape uses 16:9; 1080 px wide is a common working width; a wrong ratio forces cropping, bars, or stretching; the right ratio fills more screen and can improve engagement; and image specs 'change... a lot' as networks alter how images display, so designers should not memorize dated pixel numbers.
